lesson.title: Splitting Without Separating: Sympatric Speciation
lesson.summary: Sympatric speciation is the formation of new species within the same geographic area, without a physical barrier to gene flow, driven by mechanisms such as polyploidy, host or habitat specialization, and strong nonrandom mating.
lesson.body:
Sympatric speciation is defined by contrast with the allopatric mode you just studied. The Greek prefix "sym" means "together," and sympatric speciation refers to new species arising from populations that remain in the same geographic area the entire time, with no physical barrier ever separating them. This immediately raises a hard question: if the diverging groups are living side by side and are capable of encountering one another, what stops gene flow from constantly blending them back together before real differences can build up? Biologists have identified a few well supported mechanisms that answer this question, and each one works by creating something like an internal barrier to gene flow even in the complete absence of geography.

The clearest and most mechanistically simple route to sympatric speciation is polyploidy, a change in chromosome number, most often a doubling of the entire genome. This is especially well documented in plants. If an individual's chromosome number suddenly doubles, whether through an error in cell division or through hybridization between two species followed by genome doubling, that individual usually cannot produce fertile offspring by mating with the original diploid population, because their chromosomes cannot pair up evenly during meiosis. This is exactly the same chromosome pairing problem that makes mules sterile, a postzygotic barrier, except here it appears instantly, in a single generation, and it appears within a population that never moved anywhere. If the new polyploid individual can reproduce with itself or with other polyploid individuals, for instance through self pollination, common in plants, a new species can form in essentially one step. This is not a rare curiosity, a substantial fraction of flowering plant species show evidence of polyploidy somewhere in their evolutionary history, and researchers have directly documented new polyploid species forming within recorded history, including species in the genus Tragopogon (goatsbeard) that arose in North America within the past century after different Tragopogon species, introduced from Europe, hybridized with one another.

A second, more gradual sympatric pathway involves host or habitat specialization combined with strong assortative mating, meaning individuals preferentially mate with others that share their traits. The most studied example is the apple maggot fly, Rhagoletis pomonella, in North America. This fly's ancestral population fed and mated exclusively on the fruit of native hawthorn trees. When apple trees were introduced to North America, some flies shifted to feeding and laying eggs on apples instead. Because these flies mate on or near the fruit their larvae develop in, and because apple and hawthorn fruits ripen at different times of year, flies that prefer apples tend to mate with other apple-preferring flies, and flies that prefer hawthorn mate with other hawthorn-preferring flies. This is not a new chromosome number, it is host fidelity combined with a difference in timing acting as an emerging behavioral and temporal barrier, the same kinds of prezygotic barriers you studied earlier, except that here they are arising within a single interbreeding population rather than being imported from a pre-existing geographic split. Researchers regard the apple-feeding and hawthorn-feeding fly populations as being in an early or intermediate stage of sympatric speciation, showing measurable genetic differences and reduced interbreeding, though whether they will become fully separate species is still being studied.

A third well documented case comes from cichlid fish in small volcanic crater lakes, for example crater lakes in Nicaragua and in Cameroon. These lakes are geographically tiny and lack any internal geographic barrier, yet researchers have found multiple cichlid species within single crater lakes that are each other's closest relatives and appear to have diverged in place, driven by disruptive selection on traits like body shape and feeding structures that specialize different individuals for different food sources within the same small lake, combined with mate choice based on those same traits.

Connecting back to the barriers you studied earlier, the common thread across all of these sympatric cases is that some factor, a chromosome mismatch, a shift in host plant combined with timing, or disruptive selection on feeding and mating traits, ends up functioning like a prezygotic or postzygotic barrier even without any geography involved. This is precisely why sympatric speciation was historically more controversial among biologists than allopatric speciation: it requires reproductive isolation to build up while gene flow is still physically possible, which demands a mechanism strong enough to resist the constant blending that gene flow would otherwise cause. The examples above are considered convincing today because in each case researchers can point to a specific, identifiable barrier doing exactly that job.
